title: Summaries, probability rules and Bayes
subtitle: Squeeze a pile of numbers into two or three, then learn the few rules that govern chance — and why a positive test is usually less alarming than it sounds.

sections.title: Centre and spread
sections.body: The mean x̄ = Σx/n balances the data; the median is the middle value and ignores outliers; the mode is the most frequent. Spread is measured by the variance s² = Σ(x − x̄)²/(n − 1) and its root, the standard deviation s (same units as the data). Charts: a histogram shows shape, a box plot shows median and quartiles, a scatter plot shows pairs.

worked.why: Squared deviations: 9,1,1,1,0,0,4,16 sum to 32. Divide by n − 1 = 7.

questions.prompt: Incomes 20, 22, 25, 27, 400 (thousand). Which average describes a typical person?

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: One outlier drags the mean to 98.8 but not the median.

problems.answer: s² = 32/7 = 4.571, so s ≈ 2.14 (population formula ÷8 would give 2.0).

sections.title: Probability rules
sections.body: P(A) lies in [0, 1]; the certain event has P = 1. Complement: P(Aᶜ) = 1 − P(A). Addition: P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B). Conditional: P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B)/P(B). Events are independent when P(A ∩ B) = P(A)P(B). Counting: n! orderings, ⁿPᵣ = n!/(n − r)!, ⁿCᵣ = n!/(r!(n − r)!).

worked.why: Two fair dice. P(sum = 7): 6 of the 36 outcomes.
Given the first die is 3, only (3,4) works: 1 of 6.

questions.prompt: P(A) = 0.5, P(B) = 0.4, P(A ∩ B) = 0.2. Are A and B independent?

responses.title: A tempting idea.
responses.body: Overlap is normal; independence is about the product.

sections.title: Bayes’ theorem, by counting people
sections.body: P(A | B) = P(B | A)P(A)/P(B). The trick is to imagine 1000 people. A disease has prior 1%; the test catches 90% of cases (sensitivity) and wrongly flags 9% of healthy people (specificity 91%). Of 10 sick, 9 test positive; of 990 healthy, 89.1 also do. A positive result therefore means only 0.0917 probability of disease — most positives are false alarms because the condition is rare.

questions.prompt: Why does a 10% prior give a higher posterior with the same test?

choices.text: More of the positives come from genuinely sick people.

figures.caption: Figure 1.3.1 — rare disease
figures.note: Mint = true positives, rose = false positives among everyone who tested positive.

figures.caption: Figure 1.3.2 — prior 10 %
figures.note: Raise the prior to 10% and the same test is far more convincing.

problems.prompt: A factory’s machine A makes 60% of parts (2% defective); machine B makes 40% (5% defective). A part is defective. P(it came from A)?

sections.title: When the maths is hard, simulate
sections.body: If P(event) is awkward to derive, generate many random trials and count. Throwing random points in a unit square and counting those inside the quarter-circle estimates π/4. This run gives π ≈ 3.33 (error 0.1884); the error shrinks like 1/√n, so 100× more trials gives only 10× more accuracy.

figures.caption: Figure 1.4.1 — estimating π
figures.note: Mint points are inside the circle.

sections.title: Shape and quartiles
sections.body: Sort the data: Q1, the median Q2 and Q3 cut it into quarters; the IQR = Q3 − Q1 measures spread robustly, and points beyond 1.5·IQR from the box are flagged as outliers. A histogram that trails right is right-skewed (mean > median), as incomes are; a symmetric one has mean ≈ median.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: The long right tail pulls the mean up.

sections.title: Random variables: expectation and variance
sections.body: A random variable X assigns a number to each outcome. E[X] = Σx·P(x) is the long-run average and Var(X) = E[X²] − (E[X])². For a fair die E = 3.5 and Var = 35/12 ≈ 2.92. Linearity: E[aX + b] = aE[X] + b and Var(aX + b) = a²Var(X); for independent X, Y, Var(X + Y) = Var X + Var Y.
